issues.title: pip-compile --generate-hashes downloads every file since 7.6.1: JSON API URL lost "/pypi/" (#2429)
issues.body:
### Describe the Bug

Since 7.6.1, `pip-compile --generate-hashes` no longer gets hashes from the PyPI JSON API. It silently falls back to downloading and hashing every file of every pinned version (every platform wheel and the sdist). The hashes are still correct, but the run downloads far more data. For one of our lock files (80 packages) that is 2015 files, 6.1 GiB (the sum of the PyPI file sizes), where a few small JSON requests used to be enough.

The JSON request goes to `https://pypi.org/<name>/json`, which returns 404. The API lives at `https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json`. `PyPIRepository._get_project` (`piptools/repositories/pypi.py`) builds the URL from `_get_true_base_from_index_url()`, introduced in #2429. For `https://pypi.org/simple` and `https://pypi.org/simple/` that function returns `https://pypi.org/`. `urljoin(base, f"{ireq.name}/json")` then lacks the `pypi/` segment that `PackageIndex(...).pypi_url` used to supply.

### Suggested fix

In `_get_project`:

```python
json_url = urllib.parse.urljoin(index_base_url, f"pypi/{ireq.name}/json")
```

With this one-line change, pip-tools 7.6.2 with pip 26.3 prints no `Hashing` line, both with the default index and with `https://pypi.org/simple/`, and writes the same hashes. For an index URL that ends in `/simple`, it also yields the same JSON URL as before #2429 (`<base>/pypi/<name>/json`).

The fallback is silent today. A debug or warning message when the JSON lookup returns 404 would have made this visible.

Dependabot's pip-compile updater pins pip-tools 7.6.1 (dependabot-core `python/helpers/requirements.txt`), so its `--generate-hashes` updates are affected too.

### Expected Behaviour

Hashes for packages on PyPI come from the JSON API, as in 7.6.0: no `Hashing ...` lines and no file downloads.

### Steps to Reproduce

```
python3.14 -m venv v && v/bin/python -m pip install pip==26.3 pip-tools==7.6.2
echo 'idna==3.20' > a.in
v/bin/pip-compile -v --generate-hashes a.in 2>&1 | grep Hashing
```

Output:

```
    Hashing idna-3.20-py3-none-any.whl
    Hashing idna-3.20.tar.gz
```

The result is the same with pip-tools 7.6.1 and pip 26.2.1, and with `--index-url https://pypi.org/simple/`. pip-tools 7.6.0 with pip 26.1.1 prints no `Hashing` line. All runs write the same two hashes, which equal the PyPI JSON digests.

### Environment Versions

1. Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 container)
2. Python 3.14.7
3. pip 26.3 (also 26.2.1)
4. pip-tools 7.6.2 (also 7.6.1; `main` at 5e34b816 has the same code)

issues.title: pip-compile --max-rounds 0 crashes with internal error instead of clean validation error
issues.body:
**Description**

Running `pip-compile --max-rounds 0` (or any negative number, e.g. `--max-rounds -1`) accepts the invalid value and then crashes with an internal error, including a scary "this is likely a bug" style traceback.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. In a fresh clone, run `pip-compile --max-rounds 0 requirements.in`.
2. pip-compile accepts the value and then dies with a traceback instead of a clean usage error.

**Expected behaviour**

The value should be validated up front: pip-compile should reject `0` and negative values with a clean usage error (for example, reporting that `--max-rounds` must be a positive integer) and exit without a traceback.

**Environment**

Verified in a fresh clone of the repository.

comments.body:

Unfortunately, the change breaks a test which relies on being able to pass `--max-rounds 0` in order to trigger resolution failure. So we need to either reassess that test or remove it.

issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

<!--
What are you trying to do, that you are unable to achieve with pip-tools as it
currently stands?

Let's say I'm maintaining a library, and that library supports a range of underlying dependencies, not just the most recent version.  We want to test against some of those earlier versions.

We can specify this as a version inequality, like `depX >= 1.0`.

Something like `pip-compile --minimum` or `pip-compile --lowest`.  This would produce a file with `depX == 1.0`.

-->

comments.body:
First off, I'm interested in this. I do this in a number of projects and it's a manual thing to maintain; often I have it in a separate dependency group. The experience doing this is not great.

However, I'm not sure how easy this will be. pip doesn't have this feature already, do they? I plan to reach out to them to ask if they think this is possible purely by inverting something in resolvelib and/or pip.

comments.body:

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
This would require flipping what the priority/sorting preference callback in the resolvelib's resolver class implementation returns: https://github.com/sarugaku/resolvelib/blob/a0cb7c50b78028f840b238d8e1c391e0546f2325/examples/reporter_demo.py#L78.

But you're not the first one to bring this up. I've definitely thought about it myself and had conversations with people at PyCon US in the previous years. I think @Zac-HD mentioned something and maybe someone else was around, I don't remember who exactly, unfortunately. I recall some people at Google were trying some mutation testing with different versions of the libs in the deptree. I think I might've asked Pradyun what he thought.

We (or the pip tracker) may even have an existing issue about this lying around somewhere...

AFAIU, a can of worms would definitely be involved. One thing to understand is that yes, we can immediately pin the range deps to their lowest values using `==`. I think Hypothesis just does a `sed 's/>=/==/'` to generate an additional file. But if we want the depresolver to apply the “as old as possible” strategy, then it'll end up getting every single version of every single transitive dependency it encounters from the index. It'll be really slow. It might find a metadata-compatible wheel for a dependency meant for Python 0.9, having iterated to the oldest version of a pure-python package. For, some, it'll get to building wheels from sdists (and not succeeding), making the process much slower. For transitive deps with C-extensions, there's barely any of those publishing pure-python wheels as a fall-back so it'll attempt building those extensions from ages ago wasting a lot of time. This also means higher exposure to some old malicious pieces of `setup.py` and somewhat newer undetected in-tree build backend trickery.

So before this can be implemented, the scope should be realistically limited to something maintainable and safe.

comments.author: Zac-HD
comments.body:
For prior art: uv has `--resolution lowest` and `--resolution lowest-direct` and `--exclude-newer`, pip has `--uploaded-prior-to` as of iirc 25.2, and there are other-language options like Cargo's nightly `-Z minimal-versions` / `-Z direct-minimal-versions`, etc. Go modules do minimal version selection by default, and iirc that's what I was describing when we talked a while ago.  "lowest for everything" tends to produce broken environments due to bad metadata in ancient package versions though, so in practice this is not an option (not my only "aaargh go" take).

Personally I think that "each direct dep at respectively oldest allowed version, each of their transitives no newer than that version, take (oldest/newest, idk, see what happens) for transitives of multiple direct deps" would be an excellent and basically sane option to give people.

comments.body:

When I spoke with pip devs yesterday, I was given to understand that between "implementation" and "design", the hardest part of this feature is "design" or definition. As noted, there's `lowest` vs `lowest-direct` in `uv`, and true `lowest` tends to produce broken environments. `lowest-direct` is what I plan to propose; I promised to explore `uv` behaviors a bit in order to understand the space and present some idea of what `pip` (and therefore, in my framing, `pip-compile`) should do.

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
Thanks! That statement of the desired use case is actually quite helpful.

To some degree, I think we have to think about upload dates. In practice, where I have done this, I've allowed second-order dependencies to be pinned to modern versions. It works, especially with shallow and simple trees... but it's definitely not ideal.

For this case, we're trying to simulate what a downstream got at some point in the past. Their environment was initialized at some point in time with `pip install`, `pip-compile`, or something similar. Tracing versions further back in time is not what we want, and in at least some cases it leads to pathological behavior, finding ancient versions of a package.

"The latest upload date of the minimum versions of direct dependencies" is a sensible cutoff. But even finding/computing that value gets messy because that date _itself_ depends on what resolutions are valid. Requiring it to be explicitly provided sidesteps this problem, but it's non-obvious how we'd discover the value to use.
The only solution I've thought up so far is to first do a full resolution, find the versions and upload dates (possibly manually?), and then feed those dates back into a second round of resolution.

issues.title: Ensure any dependencies are pinned whenever tests run in CI
issues.body:
We already have weak pinning for `pip` itself in our tox config (`pipsupported`, `piplowest`), and the ability to run that against latest (`pipmain`). However, `pip-tools`' testsuite runs do not pin all of the secondary dependencies (`click`) and test dependencies (`pytest`, etc).

An unfortunate and ironic consequence is that pip-tools' own CI is somewhat unstable (see, for example: #2400), and may fail due to changes  in dependencies. Typically when I see surprising CI failures, I will copy and compare the tox env output to see if packages have changed as one of my first diagnostic steps.

CI should be using fixed package versions so that it is reproducible, and we should update those pins at our discretion. Unlike docs dependency pinning (found in `tox.ini` under the envname `pip-compile-docs`), this needs to iterate over supported python versions (and platforms?) when generating pins. My best example of prior art for this is what we currently have at my work: [tox envs which encapsulate per-target pinning](https://github.com/globus/globus-sdk-python/blob/c778a75a561915b6f97d0ccf13d62ab671031463/tox.ini#L108-L133).[^1]

[^1]: We don't handle platforms explicitly in this, but our deps are sufficiently multiplatform-friendly that it works. Possibly there are even better ways.

Dependabot may not handle the results correctly; it is already wrongly mangling our docs requirements. I consider fixing it (up to and including disabling it for these targets if appropriate) to be out of scope.

---

At PyCon, @moshez generously offered to look into this, present a plan, and execute if time allows. And if it sits for a while, the writeup above is all still a valid description of what I would like us to do.

@webknjaz , I'd like us to agree on an overall strategy before anyone implements anything. Otherwise, I think it's likely that we'll have unproductive efforts or people will spin their wheels a bit.

issues.title: Parallel invocations of `pip-compile --rebuild` can see partially-deleted cache directories
issues.body: As uncovered in #2380 , `pip-compile --rebuild` and the proposed `pip-lock` rely on a cache clearing mechanism (`repository.clear_caches()`) which calls `shutil.rmtree`. However, `rmtree` is not atomic, so it is possible when `pip-compile` is run multiple times for one invocation to be using the cache while the other is in the midst of deleting it.

issues.title: Is there a way to generate hashes from an existing installation?
issues.body:
Hi!

This is more of a question than an issue regarding `pip-compile --generate-hashes`: if I understand pip-compile correctly, it takes the content of - let's say - a `requirements.in` file, resolves the packages from indexes (PyPI or others) and writes the hashes it found to requirements.txt.

Is there a way to use already installed packages as a source for the hashes instead of resolving everything from the index? 

This would be useful when on-boarding legacy projects that only have a requirements.txt file so far and you want to avoid installing new packages while generating the hash-pinned requirements.txt.

comments.body:

issues.title: [CI] Add arm workers for Ubuntu and Windows to the matrix
issues.body:
Following up on #2079 , GitHub provides ARM boxes like `ubuntu-24.04-arm` and `windows-11-arm`.

We want to be testing on a wide array of targets, so adding these would be nice. We also need to contend with the fact that our matrix is getting really big. Especially for a project which isn't full of heavily architecture-specific code, and has a flakier-than-we'd-like testsuite.

I think adding Ubuntu & Windows ARM testing raises the priority of some existing issues to solve. These are the items I'd like us to consider as we plan:

1. Refactor the way we declare our test matrix so that we can be more selective.

I'd like to see a matrix which tests something like the following suites:
```
# ranges
Python 3.9-3.14 x Ubuntu Intel
Python 3.9-3.14 x Windows Intel
Python 3.9-3.14 x macOS ARM

# top and bottom
Python 3.9, 3.14 x macOS Intel
Python 3.9, 3.14 x Ubuntu ARM
Python 3.9, 3.14 x Windows ARM
```

If we explode out the full matrix, there are 12 more jobs in there, and it's questionable whether or not they are high value for pip-tools.

2. Make tests more stable (where possible).

This shouldn't be treated as a blocker, since we can't fully solve it in short order.
We still have flaky failures because we have tests which rely on the network and state of pypi. The bigger we make our matrix, the more important stable tests are.

3. Make tests faster (where possible).

Again, not a blocker but more important the bigger the matrix. Are we doing network IO to test something which can be tested without network IO? Can we make tests simply faster to run?
The cost of flakiness (item 2) goes down if it's very cheap and easy to rerun a failed job.

---

@webknjaz , I'm curious what you think of (1), in terms of picking a narrower slice vs testing the true, full matrix. Do you think that's a good idea?

If we had faster and more stable tests, I wouldn't hesitate to expand the matrix. But as things currently are, I'm a bit concerned that we could be making the project harder to maintain for limited gain.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
This shounds reasonable. I think we could run the full matrix in the merge queue but something faster on simple PR updates.

I also had ideas of having delayed heavy jobs in PRs so that the fast jobs would run fast and then the slow ones would only get unblocked in like 30 minutes — inspired by CPython's buildbots that run post-merge even. Although, I'd implement this through GitHub Environments with a wait timer in its protection settings — this would allow only running the fast jobs when somebody keeps pushing updates to PRs every few minutes but run everything later on, when they're settled on the implementation. This would need thinking about `alls-green` additionally, though. I haven't attempted this approach anywhere but it's been in my head for a while.

Another thing to explore is change detection w/ something like https://www.testmon.org but I know it used to be problematic when paired with coveragepy in the past.

issues.title: Reduce circular dependencies between `utils.py` and `_compat/` by migrating pip-related utilities into a new `_pip_api`
issues.body:
I've been bitten a couple of times by the circular relationship between "utils" and "_compat", and we have some old PRs which got snagged on it as well. (I was trying to port the changes in #2108 forward.) The current module structure is not right in terms of defining dependencies between components -- if you try to migrate any component from "utils" into "compat", you create cycles.
"utils" is also a generally disliked component name, since it doesn't contain important information about its contents.

Tinkering a bit in the repo today, and trying to decide on a path forward, I started to focus on the fact that `utils` and `_compat.pip_compat` are both concerned with providing an API for `pip` usages, like the `PIP_VERSION` constant.

I propose that we pursue a gradual migration:
1. We introduce `piptools._pip_api`, which is _our API_ for usage of `pip`. It is, of course, internal-only.
2. `piptools._pip_api` is defined to not have any dependencies on any other parts of `piptools` for now. i.e. We aren't going to allow the reintroduction of this kind of circular problem -- we could add smaller modules which `_pip_api` would be able to consume in the future, but the one we have to strictly rule out is `utils`.
3. As much of `utils` as is reasonable is ported into `_pip_api`, and consumption is updated.
4. Testing is also dir structured, into `tests/pip_api/test_{module_name}.py` (we have too many tests in a flat dir at present, IMO. I want some better organization to the testsuite so that I can find things).

issues.title: Include the pip-tools version in the header of pip-compiled requirements.txt files
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

It can be useful to replicate the `pip-compile` environment previously used to autogenerate a `requirements.txt` file.  In particular: re-using the same version of `pip-compile` is likely to minimise the effect of any other local changes applied.

To phrase that conversely: when people attempt to regenerate a `requirements.txt` file using a much more recent version of `pip-tools`, it's likely that the output will include extraneous differences that may make it more difficult to notice any unrelated/unexpected changes.

It is currently not readily apparent from the contents of a `pip-compile`'d `requirements.txt` file what version of `pip-tools` was used to compile it.

An optional header can be added, but it contains only the major/minor Python version used, but not the `pip-tools` version.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like to suggest adding the `pip-tools` version to the header output when the `--header` option is provided to `pip-compile`.

As a real-world example, to support some commentary in #2245 I'd like to try replicating the `docs/requirements.txt` file used in this repository.  It is non-trivial for me to figure out what version of `pip-tools` was used, and that makes it more difficult for me to respond in a timely and accurate manner.

The version number could be the same one produced by `pip-compile --version` -- e.g. the `7.5.1.dev42+dirty` below:

```sh
$ pip-compile --version
pip-compile, version 7.5.1.dev42+dirty
```

#### Alternative Solutions

Add `pip-tools` to `pyproject.toml` and suggest/require that developers use this version when updating autogenerated files.

This could be supported by a continuous integration check that notifies when the compiled `requirements.txt` content diverges from the version committed to the source repository.

#### Additional context

Somewhat similar to #2168, except that that issue suggests adding a timestamp; I think that could be useful in some circumstances, but for the use case here I would prefer a version number.

comments.author: shivamtiwari3
comments.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful review of #2352. I'd like to re-engage on this properly by answering your questions before any code is written.

**1. Should `pip-compile` do this at all?**

I think yes, for reproducibility. The header already includes the Python version for exactly this reason — if you pick up someone else's `requirements.txt` you can tell *what Python* compiled it. But you still can't tell *what pip-tools version* compiled it, which matters because pip-tools itself affects resolution (e.g. constraint handling, annotation format, default flags). Lockfile tools like Poetry and PDM embed their own version in their lock files for the same reason. The pip-tools header is the natural place to do this.

**2. Should the behavior be always-on, opt-in, or opt-out?**

I'd argue **always-on** when `--header` is enabled (which is the default). Reasons:
- `--no-header` already exists as a complete escape hatch for users who don't want any tooling metadata in their output.
- Adding a separate `--no-pip-tools-version` flag introduces combinatorial complexity (`--header` × `--[no-]pip-tools-version`) for a minimal benefit.
- The Python version is already always-on, so the pip-tools version is a natural peer.

Opt-out via a new flag is viable but feels over-engineered given that `--no-header` already covers the "I don't want tool metadata" use case.

**3. Should `pip-compile` update the header when the pinned requirements do not change, but the current version does not match the one in the header?**

Yes — the header should be updated. If I compiled with `7.4.0` and re-run with `7.5.0` with the same inputs, the header currently says `7.4.0` which is inaccurate. Since the purpose of recording the version is reproducibility, a stale version number is worse than no version number at all. pip-compile already rewrites files when anything changes; a version mismatch in the header should count as a change.

---

Happy to implement this if the above reasoning aligns with your thinking. I'll follow the proper contribution workflow (PR template, changelog entry, tests for the new header format and the version-mismatch rewrite scenario).

comments.body:
I remain extremely skeptical about the utility and benefit of this feature, vs the noisy annoyance that it would be for many users.

I use Poetry pretty heavily at $WORK, and I find the version number changing in the lockfile to be noise -- it has never (in 7+ years of using Poetry) been significant in tracking down a bug. Perhaps that's just a limitation of my own experience.

I've never seen anyone recording their `pip-tools` version in a file, which is already possible today.
For example, are there `justfile`s, `Makefile`s, or `tox` or `nox` configurations in which people run `pip-compile --version > .pip-tools-version.txt`? If the version number is important to record, people would already be recording it, wouldn't they?

It is not valid to treat the Python version as analogous. That goes into marker evaluation. That analogy is an argument for having a mode to record all of the marker environment information, like the platform, arch, etc. And if variants are standardized, fully recording the environment becomes genuinely impossible, so I'm not sure that it's wise to pursue.

issues.body:
So I was trying to work out how to organize interaction between tox and pip-tools for my new/future `tox-lock` plugin where I'd generate constraint files for tox environments.

I figured I'd try making a named pipe in tox's tmp dir and pass that as an input to `pip-compile`. Then, I'd write whatever's necessary from the tox plugin into the pipe and be done with it. What could go wrong, right?

When I started testing `pip-compile` even w/o tox in the mix, it was hanging on me.

Eventually, I started running the editable install of pip-tools and stuck `breakpoint()` into a couple of places. I've found out that it reads from the pipe just fine for the first time. It goes through the dependency resolution and all's good.

It's when it gets to writing the output, the problems begin. `_determine_linesep(strategy="preserve", filenames=('-', './named-pipe'))` gets called with the default `"preserve"` strategy. And in this mode, it attempts opening the file by path in binary mode, getting stuck on `existing_file.read()`:
https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/blob/78f18e11386c3c696da4ede645bf082925f8aae5/piptools/scripts/compile.py#L60

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type: Gentoo Linux (shouldn't be relevant)
1. Python version: `3.13.7` (shouldn't be relevant)
1. pip version: `25.2`
1. pip-tools version: `main` (78f18e11386c3c696da4ede645bf082925f8aae5)

#### Steps to replicate

*(\*NIX instructions)*

1. `mkfifo -m0600 named-pipe`
2. `python -m piptools compile -o- ./named-pipe`  <-- this is where it gets stuck
3. *(in a separate terminal tab)* `echo build > named-pipe` <-- this unblocks reading the file contents for the first time and lets `pip-compile` compute the dep tree, then getting stuck in `_determine_linesep()`
4. another `echo build > named-pipe` unblocks `pip-compile` because it's able to read something from the pipe again

#### Expected result

It shouldn't hang.

#### Actual result

It does.

-----------

Since I'm writing to stdout, the first loop iteration in `_determine_linesep()` gets a "file not found" and skips to the second iteration that gets stuck. It also occurred to me that if a file called `-` were to exist, it'd mess up the linesep detection since it just reads from stdin at the beginning but there, it'd read from a file. This is a loosely related bug, I suppose.
I've tested that it's possible to identify a named file programmatically though `stat` or `pathlib`, but maybe this needs a more generic "is file" check.

-> breakpoint()

{'filenames': ('-', './named-pipe'),

 'strategy': 'preserve'}
(Pdb) pp os.path.isfile(fname)
False
(Pdb) pp os.path.isjunction(fname)
False
(Pdb) pp os.path.islink(fname)

(Pdb) pp os.path.ismount(fname)

comments.author: Mukller
comments.body:
Root cause and fix:

`_determine_linesep()` with `strategy="preserve"` iterates over output filenames and calls `open(fname, "rb").read()` to detect existing line endings. For regular files this is fine. For named pipes (FIFOs), `open()` succeeds (a FIFO is openable), but `.read()` then **blocks indefinitely** — the pipe was already fully drained during the initial parse step, so there is no data and no EOF.

The regression was introduced in #1652 (v6.10.0) when `_determine_linesep()` was added. Before that, the linesep logic didn't exist, so FIFOs as input worked fine.

**Fix:** guard the `open()` with `Path(fname).is_file()`, which returns `True` only for regular files and `False` for FIFOs, sockets, directories, and non-existent paths. `Path` is already imported in `compile.py`:

```diff
 if strategy == "preserve":
     for fname in filenames:
         try:
+            if not Path(fname).is_file():
+                continue
             with open(fname, "rb") as existing_file:
                 existing_text = existing_file.read()
-        except FileNotFoundError:
+        except OSError:
             continue
```

The `except FileNotFoundError` is also broadened to `except OSError` to handle permission errors, broken symlinks, and other IO failures that could arise despite the `is_file()` pre-check (race conditions, network filesystems, etc.).

I have a PR ready.

`pip-sync` uninstalls non-matching packages which it finds in the environment. So it looks at what's installed (as you might see from `pip freeze`), excludes `pip`, `pip-tools`, and several others from the list, and marks what it finds for removal.

The main difference between the two invocations -- as far as a user of `pip` is concerned -- is that `python -m pip` finds the first `python` in your path, then looks for `pip` from there, whereas invoking `pip` directly looks for the first `pip` script/shim in your path. Most scenarios in which these don't point to the exact same code are some flavor of "broken environment", far beyond the scope of this discussion.

---

I don't think your reasoning against `pip-tools` upgrading itself is solid, since you're talking about what happens today -- which I agree is not good. And it looks to me like you have some incorrect information about how `pip` behaves which is misleading you. IMO the best resolution is to develop more correct behavior for this scenario, and that the result will be that `pip-tools` can upgrade or downgrade itself via `pip-sync`.

In any case, I agree that the docs are at best misleading and at worst outright wrong.
And we can treat this report partly as a doc enhancement request.

Expect the same behavior as the following command.

```shell
pip-sync requirements_lock.txt
```

#### Actual result

The behavior is actually equivalent to the following command.

```shell
pip-sync requirements.txt
```

#### My suggetion

The following fix will result in the expected behavior.

https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/compare/e4ed0c1e028d1ca73673a51722ba153f0c02b0c6...takuminakaso:pip-tools:ba97901e4b31731259f9da1d2a8bddcd527adcae

comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
I agree with the OP here that this is surprising and should be improved. Unfortunately, it also seems to be attracting some slop PRs.

Improving this requires some care, in that `src_files` can, unfortunately, be specified in config such that it would apply _both_ to `pip-compile` and `pip-sync` -- which makes no sense.

For example, consider this config:
```toml
[tool.pip-tools]

```

I think a good change has to narrowly load `src_files` for `pip-sync` only from `tool.pip-tools.sync`.

issues.title: pip-compile incorrectly indicates packages were not pinned
issues.body:
Pinning `setuptools` causes a warning indicating that `setuptools` was not pinned.

#### Environment Versions

1. OS Type  **Linux**
1. Python version: `$ python -V`  **3.11.9**
1. pip version: `$ pip --version`  **25.0**
1. pip-tools version: `$ pip-compile --version`  **7.4.1**

#### Steps to replicate

1. Create `requirements.in` with the following content:
```
flask==3.1.0
```
2. Attempt to generate requirements.txt: `pip-compile --generate-hashes --output-file=requirements.txt requirements.in`
3. Observe success and no warning (as expected)
4. Determine current working version of `setuptools`: `pip list | grep setuptools` (mine is 75.8.0)
5. Pin `setuptools` in `requirements.in` by changing its content to:
```
flask==3.1.0
setuptools==75.8.0
```
6. Attempt to generate requirements.txt: `pip-compile --generate-hashes --output-file=requirements.txt requirements.in`

#### Expected result

Success, or at least warnings that make sense.

#### Actual result

```
# WARNING: The following packages were not pinned, but pip requires them to be
# pinned when the requirements file includes hashes and the requirement is not
# satisfied by a package already installed. Consider using the --allow-unsafe flag.
# setuptools
The generated requirements file may be rejected by pip install. See # WARNING lines for details.
```

This warning is extremely surprising since the change that elicits this warning is pinning the very package that the message claims was not pinned.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body:
@jeffrecode historically, `setuptools` (and a few other things) used to be very tightly coupled with the ecosystem and was special-cased. It also used to be bundled in CPython's stdlib up until Python 3.12 (via `ensurepip`). There was no separation between the environment where sdists were being built and installed. It was considered a build toolchain component that one wouldn't want to *install* into their final venvs.

Nowadays, you also shouldn't install it in the same env you have a build frontend in (like `pip`, `uv`, `hatch` etc.), unless you have it as a *runtime* (not just *build*) dependency.

When building libraries, modern packaging tooling will populate ephemeral build envs somewhere in `/tmp` whenever an sdist needs to be built (usually, when a project on PyPI doesn't have a compatible wheel published). That's where `[build-system].requires` is getting installed, and that env is then destroyed. It is separate for each individual sdist it encounters. Most of the time, the only dependency you'll have there will be `setuptools` and nothing else (unless you go for using some other build backend, of course). Pip is not needed in there, as the env is populated by external tooling (the build frontend of your choice).
So when building distributable libraries, you'll use the `[build-system]` section to specify the build env and the `[project]` table to specify core packaging metadata that will end up in `.tar.gz` (sdist) and `.whl` (binary distribution) files. This is what those dependencies describe. They are abstract and must not be restrictive (not even upper bounds!), since your library will be installed in virtualenvs with other things, and you don't want to cause trouble due to dependency conflicts.

When describing the virtualenv state, though, you don't really focus on packaging a library. Yes, you may happen to install that library, but oftentimes you'll install other things. And everything in that env has to be compatible. The installer will perform dependency resolution to identify the exact concrete versions of everything in a way that there's no conflicts. That collection of projects that are coming from the list of dependencies you're installing (possibly including your library) and their transitive requirements is what makes up a venv. And this is what you want to extract from pip-tools. It sounds like in your case you didn't really intend to package your thing. So its type is not a library but an app, which roughly corresponds to a venv. And that's what you want pinned, not your direct dependency definitions (the inputs). So using the `[project]` table is not right for this.

The modern way of listing the direct dependencies (things that you import in your code) is called “dependency groups” and there's a tracking issue for adding support for this mechanism: #2062. Meanwhile, you can fall back on the pip-specific convention called `requirements.txt`. With pip, you can do `pip install --group=group-name` (since pip 25.1, it's pretty fresh!) and there's also a thing called “constraints” that has the same syntax as `requirements.txt` but a little more limited. You could use it as `pip install --group=group-name --constraint=constraints.txt`. Constraints aren't requests to install something, but rather limitations applied when the dependency resolver encounters projects listed in there. Unfortunately, the current depresolver in pip has a bug that makes it impossible to use `--hash` with constraint files: https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/9243.
So if you're using a typical pip-tools convention of `requirements.in` + `requirements.txt` (`pip-compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt`) and attempt to use it as it's meant to be via `pip install -r requirements.in -c requirements.txt`, it'll error out. By the way, if you have a pair of files like that (`.in` + `.txt`), Dependabot knows to use `pip-tools` for managing them for you.

This forces you to request installing things from what was meant to be your constraint file: `pip install -r requirements.txt` (generated from a `requirements.in`), which is effectively what people do now.

This all is to say that you should probably migrate to pairs of in+txt files. Here's an example of how PyPI uses this pattern: https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/tree/497da53/requirements.

Now, back to that `[build-system]` thing. If you do indeed have a library you distribute and need it, we can extract such dependencies from there (including the ones defined dynamically through PEP 517 / 660 hooks) via something like `--all-build-deps` or similar (https://pip-tools.rtfd.io/en/stable/cli/pip-compile/).

But this is only for your library and not for those libs that are your transitive deps. Also, if you get into the situation where you hit building from sdist, the CLI-passed `--constraint` isn't applicable to the isolated ephemeral build env I was mentioning earlier. This is a limitation of pip (https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/8439). But there's a hack that you can set the `PIP_CONSTRAINT` environment variable instead, and it'll leak into the subprocess that populates those envs: https://pip-tools.rtfd.io/en/stable/#maximizing-reproducibility.

That said, if you put build backends like `setuptools` into the same output file and `pip install -r` it, you'll probably end up with more things in your venv than you wanted. So I personally generate those separately. Especially since using `PIP_CONSTRAINT` means that you can't pass files with `--hash` in them, or it'll explode.

Admittedly, this is a bit tedious, and it'd be nice if somebody picked up that pip bug. Plus, we also have a new standard for lock files now that's also awaiting implementation: #2124.

---

To summarize: yes, you do need `--allow-unsafe` so that historically special-cased projects would end up in the output. But I'd recommend specifically separating the build env deps (if you do need them) and producing a no-hash file for just that (unless you want to manage your PEP 517 env manually in case you have control over it).

---

One last note: many people will also tell you to use `pip install --prefer-binary` or even `--only-binary=:all:` so that the depresolver will avoid sdists. This could be a nice speedup for the installer too, but on rare occasions it's not really possible (when projects only have sdists for your runtime).

comments.body:
(1) Yes, "Applications" and "Packages" are different "kinds of things", and the Python ecosystem only has its own standardized tooling right now really well built out for "Packages".

As a result, when you have an application, the toolchain can be very confusing. One of the side-effects of having package-oriented tooling is that lots of people are making their applications into packages, even though they don't technically need to. It might be "wrong" in terms of purity, but it's practical in a lot of cases because it gets you better tool support. Plus, it's a hard difference to explain, so lots of folks don't even think about the fact that there is a difference.

It's not obvious when someone shows up with an application (e.g., as you said, a Django web API) that it _shouldn't_ be a package. But it's equally non-obvious that it _should_ be one.

---

(2) I'm not sure if `pip-compile` is in any way problematic as regards package hashes. I'm slightly concerned if that's your takeaway. Typically, you can take the output of `pip-compile` and pass it to `pip install -r` or `pip-sync` and it works.

There are some subtleties about the exact behavior, and `-c` for constraints files. But if you're trying to break into the ecosystem as a new user, I'd try `pip-compile` to produce a "lock" and `pip install -r` to install from it.
You can come back to the more advanced modes of use later.

---

(3) Seems like something was lost in translation. I recommend reading [the start of the Dependency Groups specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-groups/#dependency-groups).[^1]

[^1]: I'm the author of a lot of the Dependency Groups content, including the spec. If it's not clear to you -- even as a new user -- from the intro, please let me know. I care a lot about it. ❤️ 

---

(4) Maybe! You can use `requirements.in` + `pip-compile` and have a good experience.

There's a lot -- many people say too much -- user choice in Python packaging. Often, the best way I've seen people figure out what works is to try something out, narrowly following the guidance for that toolchain, and only later think about switching. Changing between `pip-tools` and the alternatives is generally pretty easy, so I'd say it's at least a reasonable starting point.

If you're using `pip-tools`, I recommend starting with a `requirements.in`, not a `pyproject.toml`. You _may_ want a `pyproject.toml` as well or instead, but it's hard for me to guess from where I'm sitting.

---

(5) Yep! And you may care about that. Or, similarly, `--only-build-deps`. But you only need those if you're building a package, and it doesn't _sound like_ you are.

---

(6) I wouldn't call what you're seeing a limitation or a hack, just a natural (if sometimes unfortunate) consequence of how things work.

`pip-compile --constraint` is for controlling resolution behavior within the process.

Unfortunately, sometimes "just" resolving packages still requires a build step because a package is only available as source code, and it needs to be built in order to even read dependency data. When doing these builds -- ideally this never happens but there are lots of ways it can -- `pip` sets up an isolated environment to do the build. Isolation of the build environment carries some inherent meaning, part of which is that a lot of the current process context is removed as `pip` launches a subprocess.

`PIP_CONSTRAINT` is an environment variable, and on all supported platforms environment variables are passed from a process to its subprocesses. So if you set `PIP_CONSTRAINT`, those isolated builds will "get that data".

`PIP_CONSTRAINT` is therefore documented, supported, non-hacky, and means something subtly different from `--constraint` as passed on the command line.

There _is_ a `pip` bug with `PIP_CONSTRAINT` + `--hash`, that part is just an unfortunate truth. 🥲 

---

(7) PEP 751 provides for a standardized lockfile format, and is already accepted and tools are starting to implement it.
I wish I could tell you exactly how that will integrate with `pip-tools`, but we still need to work that out.

For your specific case, it's probably not relevant yet. When it is, maybe you'll want to use a `pylock.toml`, maybe not. But some of the above, like `PIP_CONSTRAINT` behavior, is probably not going to change in related ways.

---

(8) I think `--allow-unsafe` will become the default soon, and is appropriate for libraries and applications.

The question you need to answer is therefore a separate one: do you depend on `setuptools`?
If you do, you _need_ `--allow-unsafe` today to get the right behavior.
If you don't, don't worry about this and don't put `setuptools` in your requirements.

---

(9) Yep! It also matters a lot if you're using a private (e.g., corporate) mirror of the packages, since _they_ may only provide some subset of things.

comments.body:
Meta/aside: I'd like to get you some more info and then possibly mark our discussion posts as off-topic, as they don't have tremendous bearing on the original issue and it will make things easier for future readers to navigate.

> But my web API should _definitely not_ be constructed as a package, right? (No need to further educate me; I'll go do the leg work. I just want to make sure I've got the top-line from you guys.)

No, I wouldn't say "definitely not". At $WORK, we have several web APIs which _are_ built as packages.
We do this because packages are the only type of project understood by `poetry`, which was the tool selected for those applications (at the time, `poetry`, `pdm`, and `pipenv` were the mainstream tools which supported locking). It's totally fine to do it.

The fact which makes this _so_ hard to communicate well is that a lot of packaging is up to you as a user, and I feel it's misleading to say "should" or "should not". There are tradeoffs.

Most Python users are perfectly happy to build packages and use packaging as a way of organizing their software _as long as they never have to think too hard about it_. You're asking about the details though, and the details are super messy.[^1] 😅 

[^1]: Also, notably, paradigm-wise `pip-tools` exposes you to all of the details. Other tools, like `uv`, `poetry`, and `pdm` try to abstract away a lot of these details so that you never see them.

I don't want to get bogged down too much in each detail, and maybe I made a mistake trying to go item-by-item. I think we're ending up going deep on this because you're asking about `setuptools`, and you were including it in your requirements. I _don't think_ that's what you want. You wrote as one of your versions:
```toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "dockerized-api-drf"
version = "0.0.1"
dependencies = [
    "django==5.2.4",
    "build==1.2.2.post1",
    "click==8.2.1",
    "packaging==25.0",
    "pip==25.0",
    "pip-tools==7.4.1",
    "pyproject_hooks==1.2.0",
    "setuptools==80.9.0",
    "wheel==0.45.1",
]
```

`build-system` looks reasonable to me here. `project` needs `name` and `version`. `project.dependencies` looks strange to me though. You're probably using `django` for your application, and you _might_ be using `click`, but you might not, since some of those other tools use it. All of the other packages listed are components typically involved in building a package or environment, and usually not direct dependencies of a project.

Let's assume that you really want `django` and `click` just for the sake of argument. I'd expect the `project` table to look something like this:
```toml
[project]
name = "dockerized-api-drf"
version = "0.0.1"
dependencies = [
    "django >= 5.2.4",
    "click >= 8.2.1",
]
```

Note that I wouldn't typically pin them here, since pinning exact versions of things is one of the jobs that `pip-compile` excels at.

You then have _two_ goals when pinning dependencies:
1. Pin dependencies for your project, to make installation (once built) reproducible
2. Pin dependencies for the build process, to make package building reproducible

(1) is pretty simple here. `pip-compile -r ./pyproject.toml` will generate pinned versions of `django` and `click`. You can add hashes, add `--require-binary :all:`, and pass that data to `pip install -r`. Done!

For many Python users, this is where their investigation into this matter stops, until _sooner or later_ a new version of `setuptools` releases and something subtle breaks. Because we haven't pinned the version of `setuptools` yet, when the build step happens for `dockerized-api-drf`, the latest version of `setuptools` will be fetched.

We can, since we're looking directly at the problem, do a bit better. To pin the build dependencies, the simplest thing is to only ask for pinning of the content in the `build-system` table. For example, with
```
$ pip-compile -r ./pyproject.toml --only-build-deps --build-deps-for wheel --allow-unsafe
```
Your output will be something like
```
# The following packages are considered to be unsafe in a requirements file:
setuptools==80.9.0
    # via dockerized-api-drf (pyproject.toml::build-system.requires)
```

That output would be viable for use with `PIP_CONSTRAINT` when building your package.
Once you have the build dependencies pinned, you can then call `pip wheel . --no-deps` or use `python -m build` -- whatever way you want to build your package.

Conceptually this is a distinct thing to pin vs your package requirements -- you're pinning the build requirements.
It might be tempting to put everything together with something like
```
$ pip-compile --build-deps-for wheel --allow-unsafe -r ./pyproject.toml -q
```
but this gets just a little bit dicey.

Because it mixes together the things you need for a build with the things you actually need installed in your application's environment, if you `pip install -r` the result, you'll get `setuptools` in addition to `django` and `click`. It might be harmless, but it's a bit messy. And there are cases where it could cause issues or even breakage. Imagine what would happen if `setuptools` also depends on `click`, but requires `click < 8.2` -- suddenly things can't be installed together because we've created a conflict.

So here's one path:
- pin the build requirements in one file
- pin the package requirements in a separate file
- use the build requirements with `PIP_CONSTRAINT` to build your package
- use the built package with `pip install --no-deps` to install your built package
- use the package requirements with `pip install -r` to install your dependencies

Here's a different path:
- only pin the package requirements
- use those package requirements with `pip install -r`
- install your package with `pip install --no-deps`, allowing `pip` to do the build without enforcing reproducibility
- use another layer of your application stack (e.g. container builds) to control for the mild level of non-reproducibility

There are many other ways to navigate this. For example, I didn't suggest doing anything to control the version of `pip` or `build` which you might be using. You can pin those too. I wouldn't look at this as a maze, but more like something with layers or depth -- you can go deeper and deeper on reproducibility, depending on how strong your needs are.

Hey @jeffrecode, Stephen shared excellent insight and I wanted to add a few notes. As for moving this elsewhere, I think we should look into enabling the GitHub Discussions tab in this repo (I'll ask Jannis). Alternatively, come talk to us over on matrix.

----

> But my web API should _definitely not_ be constructed as a package, right?

One of the cases where you'd *have to* make it packaged is when you're building a [Django App](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/intro/reusable-apps/) that you might want to build into multiple standalone web APIs. This is because you'd need to make it installable into other projects so that `pip install` would place them under `site-packages/` of their respective virtualenvs. You could version them and publish to package indices (PyPI or company-internal), or just having other projects `pip install path/to/folder/git/or/whatever`. Unless the installable artifact is a wheel already, any other `pip install` invocations *always* make a wheel first, from whatever you supply.
In this case, you'd have a `pyproject.toml` for your reusable app and maybe multiple `requirements.in` files for various development workflows (testing/linting/docs) for that app. But the web API projects would not need it and could just rely on `requirements.in` what would point to your app. My current preference is going this way to describe what should go into your virtualenvs (which might include your reusable app, but also might not). The “lock files” just add another dimension to pin those virtualenvs.


> I honestly don't get it:
>
> ```console
> # WARNING: The following packages were not pinned, but pip requires them to be
> # pinned when the requirements file includes hashes and the requirement is not
> # satisfied by a package already installed. Consider using the --allow-unsafe flag.
> ```

So basically if you `pip install -r requirements.in` and `requirements.in` contains at least a single entry with `--hash`, but at least one project it needs to install *(this could be either a direct entry in `requirements.in` or transitive, like a dependency of a dependency)* does not have a `--hash`, it'll refuse to complete the installation request since you imply you want hash-checking but don't provide hashes for *everything*.
Additionally, due to historical reasons, `pip-compile --no-allow-unsafe` is still the default (we'll change that!) and excludes `setuptools` (and a few other things) from the output, basically getting you into trouble with `pip install` when combined with `--generate-hashes`. And it's trying to warn you about this quirk. It's only output because `setuptools` is *somewhere* in your dependency tree (in your case, you were declaring it your direct dependency).

You shouldn't need to depend on `setuptools` unless you're building something in the packaging space (like a plugin for `setuptools` itself). There used to be things that it provided through `pkg_resources` (which is one of the importables `setuptools` provides) but most stuff you'd use that for is available in stdlib via `importlib.resources` nowadays.

As for the very last example you posted, the reason is all the same and a TL;DR would be to just add a `.pip-tools.toml` into your project copying the one I linked above (maybe just drop the `generate-hashes` bit since you want the opposite).

P.S. Since you're talking about the reproducibility, I'd recommend making sure that you use the same Python interpreter under exactly the same OS and CPU architecture for running `pip-compile` and `pip install` as these factors will often impact the shape of your dependency tree.

issues.title: Multiple hashes per release without comments makes --generate-hashes outputs hard to audit.
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

When I run pip-compile --generate-hashes and suggest its output to update a repository's dependencies, it needs to get reviewed. The fact that the `--hash` output strings are alphabetically sorted makes its deterministic, but not in an auditable fashion. If I say, here's greenlet-3.1.1's hashes, and there are 30-some odd digests, a meticulous reviewer will need to go double-check each digest or complain that there are too many and that we only need to support x,y,z platforms, so drop unnecessary trust in other digests.

#### Describe the solution you'd like

Since line continuation syntax makes commenting each hash "line" hard to contextualize with a comment that provides the release archive's file name it corresponds to, I'd ask that --generate-hashes produce its hashes in the order that the files appear on the release page: Source tarball, then each binary distribution tarball in displayed order.

I'm recommending software supply chain integrity improvements to the EDK2 firmware toolkit project since it uses Python in its build system tooling, and a supply chain attack can lead to firmware rootkits. Given the sensitive nature of firmware and this project's importance to many hardware manufacturers, reviewers set a high bar of scrutiny. Being asked to review the ~450 hash  pip-compile output for https://github.com/tianocore/edk2/blob/master/pip-requirements.txt is troublesome for these experts.

#### Alternative Solutions

* If package index release orderings are inconsistent, then generate a comment that includes the archive names that correspond to the hashes in the order they appear. I haven't experimented with index ordering as an invariant, so this may be a necessary fallback. The downside is even more verbose requirements files.

* Amend the pip requirements grammar to allow for in-place comments, like `;#(<comment>)` so the filenames can be next to their digests. This is more intrusive since it requires every pip installation to support the new syntax.

* Avoid pip-compile altogether and cherry-pick each hash I think is useful? But there are too many industry partners with development environments that may or may not require some platform that has pre-built binaries for.

issues.title: Add custom comment to excluded "unsafe" package
issues.body:
#### What's the problem this feature will solve?

Pip-compile users may consider a package to be "unsafe" to pin for a variety of reasons: e.g. necessary security patches, bloated dependency chains, multiple providers of the same python package, etc. Currently, there is no option to customize the `requirements.txt` comment indicating a package is unsafe. They all have the same header:
```
# The following packages are considered to be unsafe in a requirements file:
# opencv-python
```
From just this information, it's unclear *why* `opencv-python` is unsafe. Is there a security vulnerability? Or is a different reason as listed above?

#### Describe the solution you'd like
Ideally, each package can explain why it was excluded. As one example:

```bash
pip-compile --no-allow-unsafe \
    --unsafe-package "opencv-python  # has many providers such as  opencv-python-headless, opencv-contrib-python, etc. so no need to force a more bloated option" \
    --unsafe-package "another-package  # with it's reason for exclusion"
```

#### Alternative solutions
It would also make sense if an `--exclude` option was present instead, which generates the heading:

```
# The following packages are listed as dependencies, but explicitly excluded from this requirements file:
# package-a
```

Or something similar. I am filing this request under `allow-unsafe` instead of an additional `--exclude` flag since https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/333 is marked as closed with the suggestion people use this instead.

comments.author: webknjaz
comments.body: The solution is to list your direct deps in a `.in` file instead of the command-line. The command-line args don't usually get complicated processing, but the input files would have that. The resulting constraints `.txt` probably shouldn't contain these comments anyway. The input file is the right place for those comments.
